y-m-09-01.title: Is an angle with longer sides a bigger angle?
y-m-09-01.topic: Comparing the sizes of angles (comparing with a right-angle paper)
y-m-09-01.goal: Learn that the size of an angle is decided not by the length of the sides but by how far the two sides open, checking in the order that evidence from comparing with a right-angle paper builds up, and fixing your first judgment.
y-m-09-01.material: Mina drew two angles. Angle ㄱ has two sides of 3 cm each going out from the vertex, and angle ㄴ has two sides of 6 cm each. Mina says, "Angle ㄴ has longer sides, so it is the bigger angle." There is no picture. There is a paper folded into a right-angle shape (a right-angle paper). This paper is a tool: you match its corner to the vertex of the angle, lay one side over it, and then look at how the angle's other side lies against the paper's side. (ㄱ is read giyeok, ㄴ is read nieun, ㄷ is read digeut, and ㄹ is read rieul.)
y-m-09-01.thinking.0: Putting off a judgment when information is lacking
y-m-09-01.thinking.1: Fixing a judgment with new evidence
y-m-09-01.thinking.2: Finding cases where angles are the same even though the lengths differ, and different even though the lengths are the same
y-m-09-01.prereq.0: Pointing out the vertex and two sides of an angle (Grade 3, first semester level)
y-m-09-01.prereq.1: Placing a right-angle paper on an angle to tell apart right angles, angles bigger than a right angle, and smaller angles
y-m-09-01.prereq.2: Reading a clock at the hour (what o'clock)
y-m-09-01.s.s1.prompt: Data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your idea of which angle is bigger.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write the side lengths of angle ㄱ and angle ㄴ side by side, and write what other information besides length you need to be able to compare.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.hint.1: When placing the right-angle paper on an angle, act out with your hand how the paper's side and the angle's other side lie.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.info: What is known: The two sides of angle ㄱ are 3 cm each, and the two sides of angle ㄴ are 6 cm each. We do not yet know how far open the two angles are.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: With only what you know now, can you say which angle is bigger?
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.after: You cannot compare the sizes of two angles by side length alone. You need another way to hold the two angles against the same standard.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Angle ㄴ is bigger, because its sides are longer.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: When sides are long, the angle easily looks bigger. Think about whether the side length tells you how far open the angle is.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The two angles are the same, because each has two sides.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Every angle has two sides. This fact alone does not let you compare sizes.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.info: When I matched the corner of the right-angle paper to the vertex of angle ㄱ and laid one side over it, the other side of angle ㄱ fit exactly with the paper's other side. I did the same for angle ㄴ, and it fit exactly too.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: How can you compare the two angles with this new information?
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.after: Even though the side lengths differ, 3 cm and 6 cm, the two angles were the same size (a right angle). The first idea "longer sides mean a bigger angle" does not fit this evidence.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Angle ㄴ is bigger. Its sides are 6 cm, so it covers more of the paper.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You should compare the direction the sides lie, not the area it covers on the paper. Read the observation "it fit exactly" again.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Angle ㄱ is bigger. The short sides fit the paper better.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: What was observed is not "fits better" but "both fit exactly."
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The two angles are the same size. Both are right angles.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This thinking compares based on the result of holding them against the same standard (the right-angle paper).
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: We cannot decide yet. We have to make the sides longer and check again.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Even if you make the sides longer, the direction they lie does not change. Think about whether the observation you already have is enough.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.info: I also drew angle ㄷ and angle ㄹ. The sides of both angles are 2 cm each. When I placed the right-angle paper, the other side of angle ㄷ was inside the paper's side, and the other side of angle ㄹ was outside the paper's side.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Of angle ㄱ, angle ㄷ, and angle ㄹ, which is the biggest angle?
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.after: The two angles with the same side length of 2 cm (ㄷ and ㄹ) also had different sizes. There are angles that are the same even though the lengths differ and angles that are different even though the lengths are the same, so the size of an angle is not decided by the length of the sides.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.reflect: At first, putting off a judgment was fitting because we knew only the side lengths. When we held them against the same standard, the right-angle paper, there were angles that were the same even though the side lengths differed (ㄱ and ㄴ), and angles that were different even though the side lengths were the same (ㄷ and ㄹ). Say what information at which step changed your thinking.
y-m-09-01.s.s2.prompt: The hour hand and minute hand of a clock have different lengths. Among the hours when the minute hand points to 12, find two different times when the two hands make a right angle. (Write which o'clock it is, from 1 o'clock to 12 o'clock.)
y-m-09-01.s.s2.hint.0: Put the minute hand at 12 on the clock face, change the number the hour hand points to one at a time, and place the right-angle paper.
y-m-09-01.s.s2.hint.1: Also look at what shape it is in cases that are not right angles (when the hands form a straight line or overlap).
y-m-09-01.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an hour between 1 o'clock and 12 o'clock.
y-m-09-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please write it as a natural number from 1 to 12.
y-m-09-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The minute hand points to 12 and the hour hand points to 3 or 9, so the two hands make a right angle.
y-m-09-01.s.s2.fail.c2: At this time the two hands do not make a right angle. Place the right-angle paper on the clock shape.
y-m-09-01.s.s2.explain: At 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock, the two hands make a right angle. At 6 o'clock the two hands form a straight line, and at 12 o'clock they overlap, so they are not right angles. The lengths of the two hands differ, but the size of an angle is decided by how far open the two hands are.
y-m-09-01.s.s3.prompt: What would you like to tell Mina? Write why the size of an angle cannot be decided by the length of the sides, using the examples you found above (angle ㄱ and angle ㄴ, or the two hands of the clock).
y-m-09-01.s.s3.hint.0: Think back to the time above when the side lengths of the two angles were different but the result of placing the right-angle paper was the same.
y-m-09-01.s.s3.hint.1: First tell Mina in one sentence "what I checked," and then write the reason.
y-m-09-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Mina, even if the sides ...
y-m-09-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include an example that was the same size even though the lengths were different?
y-m-09-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write in your own words what decides the size of an angle (how far open the two sides are)?
y-m-09-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write in a tone that understands why Mina thought that?
y-m-09-01.s.s3.model.0: Even if the sides are long, the size of the angle stays the same. You have to look at how far open the two sides are. If you place the right-angle paper, the angle with 3 cm sides and the angle with 6 cm sides both fit exactly, so they are the same size.
y-m-09-01.s.s3.model.1: The size of an angle has nothing to do with the length of the sides. The hour hand and minute hand of a clock have different lengths, but they make a right angle at 3 o'clock. The angle with 3 cm sides and the angle with 6 cm sides also fit the right-angle paper in the same way.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Angle ㄱ is bigger. The shorter the sides, the more it is bent.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The sides being short does not mean it is bent more. The same goes for the sides being long.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We can't decide yet. We don't know how wide open the two angles are.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This idea treats the length of the sides and how wide the angle opens as different pieces of information.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Angle ㄷ. It is on the inner side of the paper's sides, so it opens wider.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Check by holding the paper against it whether "inner side" means it opens more or less.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Angle ㄹ. It opens out beyond the paper's sides.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This idea compared the angle that opens out beyond the sides of the right-angle paper with a right angle.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: We can't tell. The sides of the three angles are not all the same length.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Even if the sides are not the same length, you can compare using the result of holding them against the right-angle paper.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Angle ㄱ. Its side is the longest at 3 cm.
y-m-09-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The new information in this step is not the length of the sides but the result of holding them against the paper.
y-m-09-01.s.s3.model.2: Angle ㄱ has sides of 3 cm and angle ㄴ has sides of 6 cm, so the lengths are different, but both fit the right-angle paper exactly, so both are right angles. So you cannot decide the size of an angle by the length of its sides.
y-m-09-01.s.s3.model.3: The long hand and short hand of a clock are different lengths, but at 3 o'clock they make a right angle. The size of an angle is decided by how wide it opens.

y-m-09-02.title: What should the first section be to reach the running goal?
y-m-09-02.topic: Working with time shown in minutes and seconds
y-m-09-02.goal: Before finding a time, sort out what information the judgment needs, check by making them yourself that there are several records that meet the condition, and explain the slowest record (the boundary) in minutes and seconds.
y-m-09-02.material: There is a race where you run a track on the playground in two sections. Ujin set the goal of "within 3 minutes for the two sections together." (Exactly 3 minutes 0 seconds also counts as reaching the goal.) Ujin's second-section record is 1 minute 45 seconds. The first-section record is not known yet. (1 minute is 60 seconds.)
y-m-09-02.thinking.1: Finding several solutions within a limit
y-m-09-02.prereq.1: Showing time in minutes and seconds and changing units (Grade 3, first semester level)
y-m-09-02.s.s1.prompt: To judge whether Ujin reached the goal, what more do you need to know?
y-m-09-02.s.s1.hint.0: Underline what the goal is a statement about "putting together."
y-m-09-02.s.s1.hint.1: Divide the times already written in the problem from those not yet written, and write them on two lines.
y-m-09-02.s.s1.o.a: The time when the run started
y-m-09-02.s.s1.r.a: The start time alone does not tell you how long it took. A clock time and the time taken are different things.
y-m-09-02.s.s1.o.b: Ujin's record for the first section
y-m-09-02.s.s1.r.b: This thinking found which of the two sections' times to compare with the goal is still missing.
y-m-09-02.s.s1.o.c: The distance run in the second section
y-m-09-02.s.s1.r.c: The goal is about the time taken. Distance does not tell you the time taken instead.
y-m-09-02.s.s1.o.d: The records of other friends in the second section
y-m-09-02.s.s1.r.d: Other friends' records have nothing to do with the times of Ujin's two sections.
y-m-09-02.s.s1.explain: The goal is about the value of the two sections' times put together. The second-section record is given, so you need the first-section record to judge. (If you know both the start time and the end time, you can find the time taken, but the start time alone is not enough.)
y-m-09-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose a first-section record and make three different records for which Ujin reaches the goal. Conditions: the first section is 1 minute or more, and the seconds are written as natural numbers from 0 to 59 (0 included).
y-m-09-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write 3 minutes in seconds, and also change the second-section record to seconds and put them side by side.
y-m-09-02.s.s2.hint.1: After choosing one first-section record, add it to the second section and check yourself whether it is within 3 minutes.
y-m-09-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The minutes and seconds are in the right form.
y-m-09-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Write minutes and seconds as natural numbers that are 0 or more, and write seconds as 59 or less. (Example: 75 seconds is 1 minute 15 seconds)
y-m-09-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The first section is 1 minute or more.
y-m-09-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The first section must be 1 minute or more.
y-m-09-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The time of the two sections together is within 3 minutes.
y-m-09-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The time of the two sections together is over 3 minutes (180 seconds). Add it to 1 minute 45 seconds and check again.
y-m-09-02.s.s2.explain: 3 minutes is 180 seconds and the second section of 1 minute 45 seconds is 105 seconds. The first section must be 75 seconds (1 minute 15 seconds) or less and must be 1 minute (60 seconds) or more, so everything from 1 minute 0 seconds to 1 minute 15 seconds is possible. There are 16 different records.
y-m-09-02.s.s3.prompt: To reach the goal, what is the slowest the first section can be? Also write how you found out.
y-m-09-02.s.s3.hint.0: Pick the slowest record among the ones you just made, and check what happens if you add just 1 more second to it.
y-m-09-02.s.s3.hint.1: Change either 3 minutes or 1 minute 45 seconds into the other's unit and put them side by side.
y-m-09-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Can you see in your answer how 3 minutes (or 180 seconds) and 1 minute 45 seconds (or 105 seconds) were used?
y-m-09-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write how to match units when you mix minutes and seconds (such as changing to seconds)?
y-m-09-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check that at exactly 1 minute 15 seconds the total is 3 minutes and the goal is reached?
y-m-09-02.s.s3.model.0: It is 1 minute 15 seconds. 3 minutes is 180 seconds and the second section is 1 minute 45 seconds (105 seconds), so 180 minus 105 leaves 75 seconds, which is 1 minute 15 seconds.
y-m-09-02.s.s3.model.1: The first section can be up to 1 minute 15 seconds. If you rewrite 3 minutes as 2 minutes 60 seconds and take away the second section's 1 minute 45 seconds, 1 minute 15 seconds is left, so if the first section is longer than that, it goes over 3 minutes.

y-m-09-03.title: Is it really 2 km from home to the library?
y-m-09-03.topic: Units of length (km, m) and lengths measured along a road
y-m-09-03.goal: Realize that even with the same number calculation, when it is right and when it is wrong differ depending on which road's length you mean, and tell apart what you can settle and what you cannot when new information appears.
y-m-09-03.material: Hajun said, "It is 1 km 200 m from home to school, and 800 m from school to the library. So it is 2 km from home to the library!" You have not seen a map yet. All lengths are "lengths measured by walking along the road." (1 km is 1000 m. km is read kilometer and m is read meter.)
y-m-09-03.thinking.0: Finding the conditions under which a claim holds
y-m-09-03.thinking.1: Separating what you can settle and what you cannot in front of new information
y-m-09-03.prereq.0: Knowing 1 km is 1000 m and working with lengths shown in km and m (Grade 3 level)
y-m-09-03.prereq.1: Understanding the meaning of a road connecting places on a map
y-m-09-03.s.s1.prompt: In which case is Hajun's statement certainly right?
y-m-09-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write the two lengths Hajun said, each from where to where, in the order "home, school, library."
y-m-09-03.s.s1.hint.1: Draw two or three roads that "from home to the library" could mean, and check whether each road passes through both sections.
y-m-09-03.s.s1.o.a: The case where you mean the length of a new road going straight from home to the library
y-m-09-03.s.s1.r.a: You cannot know the length of the new road from this information. Look again at which road is meant.
y-m-09-03.s.s1.o.b: The case where you mean the length when the library is on the same road between home and school
y-m-09-03.s.s1.r.b: If the library is closer to home than school is, the distance from home to the library should be shorter than from home to school. This is a value that changes with the position.
y-m-09-03.s.s1.o.c: The case where you mean the length of the road from home through school to the library
y-m-09-03.s.s1.r.c: This thinking checked whether you meant one road made of the two connected sections.
y-m-09-03.s.s1.o.d: The case where you mean the length of the nearest road from home to the library
y-m-09-03.s.s1.r.d: It is not settled that the nearest road is the one that passes through school. We do not know about other roads yet.
y-m-09-03.s.s1.explain: The road walking on from home through school to the library is a road joining the two sections, so it is 1 km 200 m plus 800 m, which is 2000 m, or 2 km. If you mean other roads or other positions, you cannot say this value is right.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.prompt: The teacher told us, "A new road that connects home and the library directly has been built. We do not yet know how long that road is. Now the only roads from home to the library are two: 'the road through school' and 'the new road.'" What can you say about "the length of the shortest road to walk from home to the library"?
y-m-09-03.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine the case where the new road is very short and the case where it is very long, and write which road is the shortest in each.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.hint.1: Find out whether there is a fact that does not change no matter how long the new road is.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.o.a: It is exactly 2 km. The road through school is 2 km, so it stays the same.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.r.a: You may have missed that the new road could be shorter than 2 km.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.o.b: It is not longer than 2 km. The exact value requires knowing the new road.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.r.b: This thinking used the fact that since there is already one road we know, the shortest road cannot be longer than it.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.o.c: It is shorter than 2 km. This is because the new road goes straight.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.r.c: A road that goes straight is not always short. We do not know the length of the new road yet.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.o.d: We cannot tell. If we do not know the length of the new road, there is nothing we can say.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.r.d: Even if there is something you do not know, think about whether there is something you can say from the road you already know.
y-m-09-03.s.s2.explain: The road through school is 2 km, so the shortest road is 2 km or less. If the new road is shorter than 2 km, the shortest road is the new road, and if it is longer than 2 km, it is still 2 km. You can only say the exact value if you know the length of the new road.
y-m-09-03.s.s3.prompt: It turned out that the new road is 1 km 500 m. Write which road is the shortest to walk from home to the library, and how many m shorter it is than the road through school.
y-m-09-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write the lengths of the two roads side by side in the same unit.
y-m-09-03.s.s3.hint.1: After deciding which is longer, find out how much they differ.
y-m-09-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you decide which road is shortest by comparing the lengths?
y-m-09-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare km and m by matching them to one unit?
y-m-09-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can you explain again how you knew that the road through school is 2 km?
y-m-09-03.s.s3.model.0: The shortest road is the new road (1 km 500 m). The road through school is 2 km, or 2000 m, and the new road is 1500 m, so the new road is 500 m shorter.
y-m-09-03.s.s3.model.1: Going by the new road is the shortest. The road through school is 1 km 200 m joined with 800 m, which is 2 km, and the new road is 1 km 500 m, so the difference between the two roads is 500 m.

y-m-09-04.title: Guessing the weight of one apple with a balance scale
y-m-09-04.topic: Weight (g) and finding a range by comparing on a balance scale
y-m-09-04.goal: Even if you cannot know the exact value, state a range for the weight from the comparison results, narrow the range with new observations, and think about the limit of whether the tools you have now can narrow it further.
y-m-09-04.material:
You put an apple on one pan of a balance scale and weights on the other pan to compare. The heavier side goes down, and if the weights are equal, it is level. There are several weights each of 50 g, 100 g, 200 g, and 500 g. Say there are several apples that weigh exactly the same, and the weight of 1 apple is a natural number in g.
Observation 1: 1 apple vs. two 200 g weights → the apple side went down.
Observation 2: 1 apple vs. one 500 g weight → the weight side went down.
y-m-09-04.thinking.0: Reasoning out a range from comparison results
y-m-09-04.thinking.1: Making several values that meet all the conditions
y-m-09-04.thinking.2: Thinking about the limits of the tools and designing the next experiment
y-m-09-04.prereq.0: Knowing the meaning of g and kg and that 1 kg is 1000 g (Grade 3 level)
y-m-09-04.prereq.1: Knowing that the heavier side goes down on a balance scale
y-m-09-04.prereq.2: Comparing the sizes of numbers and saying them as "greater than, less than"
y-m-09-04.s.s1.prompt: From Observation 1 and Observation 2 alone, what can you say about the weight of 1 apple?
y-m-09-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each observation, mark which side went down, and write one line saying that side is heavier.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.hint.1: Put the two lines side by side and mark on a number line the section the apple's weight could be in.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.o.b: It is exactly 500 g, because it was compared with the 500 g weight.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.r.b: This thinking sees the weight of the weight used for comparing as the apple's weight. Look again at which side went down.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.explain: In Observation 1 the apple side went down, so the apple is heavier than 400 g, and in Observation 2 the weight side went down, so it is lighter than 500 g. We cannot yet settle the exact value, and can only say it is between 401 g and 499 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.prompt: Observation 3 has been added. Observation 3: 1 apple vs. (two 200 g weights and one 50 g weight) → the apple side went up. Write 3 different weights (g) of 1 apple that satisfy all three observations.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write each observation as "the apple's weight is heavier/lighter than ○○ g," and pick one number that satisfies all three lines.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.hint.1: Put the number you chose into the three lines in turn, and if any observation disagrees, fix it.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The weight is a natural number in g.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please write the weight as a natural number in g.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.ok.c2: It agrees with Observation 1: it is heavier than 400 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.fail.c2: It does not agree with Observation 1. The apple side went down, so it must be heavier than 400 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.ok.c3: It agrees with Observation 2: it is lighter than 500 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.fail.c3: It does not agree with Observation 2. The weight side went down, so it must be lighter than 500 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.ok.c4: It agrees with Observation 3: it is lighter than 450 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.fail.c4: It does not agree with Observation 3. The apple side went up, so it must be lighter than 450 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s2.explain: The weights that keep all three observations are natural numbers from 401 g to 449 g. With more observations the range got narrower, but it has not been settled to one value.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.o.a: It is heavier than 400 g and lighter than 500 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.r.a: This idea rewrote the side that went down and the side that went up as comparisons of numbers.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.o.c: It is exactly 450 g. It is exactly halfway between 400 g and 500 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.r.c: This idea decides it is exactly halfway between the two values. There is no evidence anywhere that it is halfway.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.o.d: We can't know anything. It has to balance to know the weight.
y-m-09-04.s.s1.r.d: Even if it does not balance, you get the information "heavier" or "lighter."
y-m-09-04.s.s3.prompt: Using only the weights we have now (50 g, 100 g, 200 g, 500 g), can we narrow the range of the apple's weight, 401 to 449 g, any further? If we can, write how to compare using numbers; if we can't, write the reason.
y-m-09-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write down all the weights you can compare with when 1 apple is put on, and check whether those weights fall within the range 401 to 449 g.
y-m-09-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write down how the weights you can compare with change when you change the number of things put on the pan.

y-m-09-05.title: Segments and rays: can we count them the same way?
y-m-09-05.topic: Telling apart segments, rays, and lines, and counting them
y-m-09-05.goal: Using the fact that segment ㄱㄴ and segment ㄴㄱ are the same but ray ㄱㄴ and ray ㄴㄱ are different, find the wrong line in a solution and find the number of points that fits the conditions.
y-m-09-05.material:
There are points ㄱ, ㄴ, and ㄷ that are not all on one straight line. (ㄱ is read giyeok, ㄴ is read nieun, and ㄷ is read digeut.)
Agreement: Segment ㄱㄴ and segment ㄴㄱ are the same segment, and line ㄱㄴ and line ㄴㄱ are also the same line. Ray ㄱㄴ is a line that starts at point ㄱ, passes through point ㄴ, and goes straight on without end, and ray ㄴㄱ is a line that starts at point ㄴ, passes through point ㄱ, and goes straight on without end.
Jia solved for the numbers of segments, lines, and rays that can be made from points ㄱ, ㄴ, and ㄷ as below.
y-m-09-05.thinking.0: Finding the line in a solution that jumps ahead with no basis
y-m-09-05.thinking.1: Thinking about which things the same method works for and which it does not
y-m-09-05.thinking.2: Finding several cases that satisfy the limits
y-m-09-05.prereq.0: The meaning and naming of segments, rays, and lines (Grade 3, first semester level)
y-m-09-05.prereq.1: Knowing that a ray is a line that starts at one point and goes straight on without end in one direction
y-m-09-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in Jia's solution. (If two lines are wrong, you may choose the first wrong line.)
y-m-09-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, check one by one whether the result counted with the same method (choosing two points) is right for segments, lines, and rays.
y-m-09-05.s.s1.hint.1: With just the two points ㄱ and ㄴ, draw a segment, a line, and a ray, and count how many different lines there are.
y-m-09-05.s.s1.line.0: There are 3 points, so the ways to choose two points are 3: (ㄱ, ㄴ), (ㄱ, ㄷ), (ㄴ, ㄷ).
y-m-09-05.s.s1.line.1: If you choose two points and draw a segment, there are 3 segments.
y-m-09-05.s.s1.line.2: If you choose two points and draw a line, there are also 3 lines.
y-m-09-05.s.s1.line.3: If you choose two points and draw a ray, there are also 3 rays.
y-m-09-05.s.s1.line.4: So there are 3 each of segments, lines, and rays.
y-m-09-05.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. Even if you choose two points, two rays are made, depending on which point it starts from. Ray ㄱㄴ and ray ㄴㄱ are different from each other. Line 5 follows the wrong conclusion of line 4, so it is wrong too. Lines 1 to 3 are right. Segment ㄱㄴ and segment ㄴㄱ are the same segment, and the same goes for lines.
y-m-09-05.s.s2.prompt: There are n points on a plane, and no three of them are on one straight line. Find two different values of n such that, with n points, the number of rays you can draw is 10 or more and the number of lines is 10 or fewer.
y-m-09-05.s.s2.hint.0: First write how many lines and rays there are with 3 points, then count how many new lines appear when you add one more point.
y-m-09-05.s.s2.hint.1: Pick one point and count how many rays start from that point, then use the fact that it is the same for every point to check the total.
y-m-09-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of points is a natural number that is 2 or more.
y-m-09-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the number of points a natural number that is 2 or more.
y-m-09-05.s.s2.fail.c2: There are fewer than 10 rays. Count what happens with one more point.
y-m-09-05.s.s2.fail.c3: There are more than 10 lines. Count what happens with one fewer point.
y-m-09-05.s.s2.explain: With 4 points there are 6 lines and 12 rays, and with 5 points there are 10 lines and 20 rays. With 3 points there are only 6 rays, and with 6 points there are 15 lines, which is over 10. So 4 and 5 fit the conditions.
y-m-09-05.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Jia. There are 3 segments, so why are there more than 3 rays? Write using ray ㄱㄴ and ray ㄴㄱ as an example.
y-m-09-05.s.s3.hint.0: If you draw ray ㄱㄴ and ray ㄴㄱ each, compare how the starting point and the direction it extends differ.
y-m-09-05.s.s3.hint.1: With 3 points, list separately the rays starting at ㄱ, the rays starting at ㄴ, and the rays starting at ㄷ.
y-m-09-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart where ray ㄱㄴ and ray ㄴㄱ start?
y-m-09-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the thought "choosing two points makes one line" is right for segments and lines but not for rays?
y-m-09-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check with numbers how many rays there are in all?
y-m-09-05.s.s3.model.0: Segment ㄱㄴ and segment ㄴㄱ are the same segment, but ray ㄱㄴ starts at ㄱ and extends toward ㄴ, and ray ㄴㄱ starts at ㄴ and extends toward ㄱ, so they are different. So each pair of points makes 2 rays, giving 6 in all.
y-m-09-05.s.s3.model.1: If the starting point is different, it is a different ray. Rays starting at ㄱ are 2, one toward ㄴ and one toward ㄷ, those starting at ㄴ are also 2, and those starting at ㄷ are also 2, so there are 6 in all, which is more than 3.

y-m-09-06.title: If we sort by "fun books," will the result be the same no matter who does it?
y-m-09-06.topic: Choosing a rule for sorting data
y-m-09-06.goal: Learn the conditions for a sorting rule that gives the same result no matter who sorts, check how the sorting result changes when you change the number in the rule, and rewrite a vague rule as a clear rule.
y-m-09-06.material:
You want to sort 10 class-library books into two shelf rows. Each book has a sorting label on its spine, and the number of pages is written on each book.
Book 1: storybook, 64 pages / Book 2: science, 120 pages / Book 3: social studies, 48 pages / Book 4: storybook, 150 pages / Book 5: science, 200 pages / Book 6: old tales, 36 pages / Book 7: science, 88 pages / Book 8: storybook, 96 pages / Book 9: diary, 24 pages / Book 10: math, 130 pages.
You want to use a rule that gives the same result even if the three students in charge of arranging them change.
y-m-09-06.thinking.0: Evaluating whether a sorting rule is clear
y-m-09-06.thinking.1: Checking that the result changes when the rule changes
y-m-09-06.prereq.0: Sorting data and counting the number in each item (Grade 3 level)
y-m-09-06.prereq.1: Reading book information such as the label on the spine and the number of pages
y-m-09-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the rules that split the 10 books into the same two shelves no matter who sorts.
y-m-09-06.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine three different people using each rule, and look for a book that the three might put on different shelves.
y-m-09-06.s.s1.hint.1: For each rule, write which part of the book you look at to sort (spine, pages, feeling, etc.) and mark the ones you can check with your eyes.
y-m-09-06.s.s1.o.a: Books that are fun to read / books that are not fun
y-m-09-06.s.s1.r.a: Fun is different for each person, so the same book could be put on different shelves.
y-m-09-06.s.s1.o.b: Books with 100 pages or more / books with fewer than 100 pages
y-m-09-06.s.s1.r.b: This thinking sorts by comparing with the number written on the book.
y-m-09-06.s.s1.o.c: Books that are easy to read / books that are hard to read
y-m-09-06.s.s1.r.c: How easy it is to read also feels different for each person.
y-m-09-06.s.s1.o.d: Books whose spine label is "science" / books that are not
y-m-09-06.s.s1.r.d: This thinking sorts by looking at the letters written on the spine.
y-m-09-06.s.s1.o.e: Books with pretty covers / books that are not pretty
y-m-09-06.s.s1.r.e: The feeling of pretty is different for each person.
y-m-09-06.s.s1.explain: The number of pages and the letters on the spine label are the same for anyone who looks, so with these two rules the result is the same no matter who sorts. Fun, easy to read, and pretty cover differ from person to person, so the result could differ.
y-m-09-06.s.s2.prompt: You decided to sort by the number of pages. Decide ㅁ in "books with ㅁ pages or more / books with fewer than ㅁ pages" and make two different ways of sorting so that each of the two shelves has 4 books or more and 6 books or fewer. (If ㅁ differs but the books are split in the same way, count it as the same way of sorting.)
y-m-09-06.s.s2.hint.0: Line up the books in order from the most pages, choose ㅁ, and draw a line under the books with that number or more.
y-m-09-06.s.s2.hint.1: If the number of books you drew a line under is fewer than 4 or more than 6, think about which way you should move ㅁ.
y-m-09-06.s.s2.var.t: ㅁ (the page number used as the rule)
y-m-09-06.s.s2.ok.c1: ㅁ is a natural number that is 1 or more.
y-m-09-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make ㅁ a natural number that is 1 or more.
y-m-09-06.s.s2.ok.c2: There are 4 or more books with ㅁ pages or more.
y-m-09-06.s.s2.fail.c2: There are fewer than 4 books with ㅁ pages or more. Try making ㅁ smaller.
y-m-09-06.s.s2.ok.c3: There are 6 or fewer books with ㅁ pages or more (and 4 or more books with fewer pages).
y-m-09-06.s.s2.fail.c3: There are more than 6 books with ㅁ pages or more. Try making ㅁ bigger.
y-m-09-06.s.s2.explain: If you put the books in order from the most pages, they are 200, 150, 130, 120, 96, 88, 64, 48, 36, 24 pages. If ㅁ is from 97 to 120, 4 books have ㅁ pages or more, if it is from 89 to 96, 5 books, and if it is from 65 to 88, 6 books. Even when ㅁ differs, it can be the same split, and if you change ㅁ, the sizes of the two shelves change.
y-m-09-06.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite the rule "fun books / books that are not fun" so that the same result comes out no matter who sorts. Write something you can check with your eyes or count in the books.
y-m-09-06.s.s3.hint.0: See whether you can change "fun" into something you can see in the books with your eyes (pages, pictures, labels, etc.).
y-m-09-06.s.s3.hint.1: Apply the rule you wrote directly to two or three of the 10 books and decide which shelf each goes on.
y-m-09-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you think about whether the rule you wrote would give the same result even if three different people used it?
y-m-09-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you actually decide which shelf two or three of the 10 books would go on by your rule?
y-m-09-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can you say what kinds of books go on each of the two shelves?
y-m-09-06.s.s3.model.0: Sort into books with 100 pages or more / books with fewer than 100 pages. You can count the number of pages by opening the book, so it is the same for anyone.
y-m-09-06.s.s3.model.1: Sort into books with "storybook" written on the spine / books without. You can check the label with your eyes.
y-m-09-06.s.s3.model.2: Sort into books with pictures / books with only words. If you open the book, anyone gets the same result.
y-m-09-06.s.s3.model.3: Divide the books into those with more than 100 pages and those without. If you open a book and count the pages, everyone gets the same number.
y-m-09-06.s.s3.model.4: Divide the books into those whose spine label says 'science' and the others. You can check the label by looking.

y-m-09-07.title: When the total in a table differs from the number of students, what went wrong?
y-m-09-07.topic: Checking the total of data organized in a table and rewriting it
y-m-09-07.goal: Realize that when the table's total differs from the number of people surveyed, you should not force the numbers to match but check against the original data, and make by yourself several fixed tables that meet the conditions to confirm there is not just one.
y-m-09-07.material:
Class 2 of Grade 3 has 28 students in all, and each student voted only once. Each chose one favorite game to vote for, and Harin organized the results in a table.
Dodgeball 10 students / Jump rope 8 students / Tag 7 students / Board games 6 students
Look at Harin's explanation.
y-m-09-07.thinking.0: Finding the line in a solution that jumps ahead with no basis
y-m-09-07.thinking.1: Comparing ways to check the cause
y-m-09-07.thinking.2: Making several fixed tables that are possible within the conditions
y-m-09-07.prereq.0: Reading the number of students for each item from a table and finding the total (Grade 3 level)
y-m-09-07.prereq.1: Knowing the survey agreement that each person is counted only once
y-m-09-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in Harin's explanation. (If two lines are wrong, you may choose the first wrong line.)
y-m-09-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write the two numbers from line 1 and line 2 side by side and find where they disagree.
y-m-09-07.s.s1.line.0: The class has 28 students, and each voted once.
y-m-09-07.s.s1.line.1: Adding all the numbers of students in the table gives 10+8+7+6=31.
y-m-09-07.s.s1.line.2: 31 people voted, so the class has increased by 3 students.
y-m-09-07.s.s1.line.3: So this table was organized correctly.
y-m-09-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. Line 1 said the class has 28 students and each voted once, so if the total is 31, it is a sign that there is a problem with the table or the survey process. It stated that students increased without checking why the total differs. Line 4 follows from it and is wrong too. The total 31 in line 2 was calculated correctly.
y-m-09-07.s.s2.prompt: To find out why the total became 31, what would be good to do first?
y-m-09-07.s.s2.hint.0: Among the choices, separate the ways that change the "facts you know now" from the ways that "check the facts again."
y-m-09-07.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether you can tell which game is wrong if you use a method that only fixes the total.
y-m-09-07.s.s2.explain: If the total does not match, do not fix the numbers first; you should check the table against the original data. If you recount the slips or check for overlapping names, you can find out where 3 extra were counted.
y-m-09-07.s.s2.acc.0: Finding students whose names overlap is also a good way to directly check why the total became greater than 28 (the case of counting twice).
y-m-09-07.s.s3.prompt: When the slips were recounted, there were cases where the same slip was counted twice. So no game increased from the number first counted, and the total became 28. Dodgeball was still more than the other games, and every game had at least one vote. Make three different fixed tables that meet all of these conditions.
y-m-09-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write how much each number in the first table can be reduced, and think about what the total of the reductions must be.
y-m-09-07.s.s3.hint.1: After making one table, check the four conditions (total, not increased, dodgeball the most, all at least 1) one at a time.
y-m-09-07.s.s3.ok.c1: Every game had at least one vote.
y-m-09-07.s.s3.fail.c1: Please write the number of students as a natural number that is 1 or more.
y-m-09-07.s.s3.fail.c2: The total is not 28 students. Add all four numbers and check again.
y-m-09-07.s.s3.ok.c3: No game increased from the number first counted.
y-m-09-07.s.s3.fail.c3: A game increased from the number first counted. Counting twice is being taken away, so it cannot increase.
y-m-09-07.s.s3.fail.c4: Dodgeball is not more than the other games.
y-m-09-07.s.s3.explain: From the first total 31, 3 students must be taken away, but which games to take how many from is not settled by this information alone. So there are several fixed tables that meet the conditions (17 in all). You can settle on one only by directly checking which slips overlapped.
y-m-09-07.s.s4.prompt: Write why the fixed table comes out in several ways, and write what you must do to settle on one of them.
y-m-09-07.s.s4.hint.0: Put two tables you made side by side and find which game's number is different.
y-m-09-07.s.s4.hint.1: Write what you cannot tell from the numbers in the table alone, and think of data that would let you know it.
y-m-09-07.s.s4.placeholder: Example: The reason there are several fixed tables is ...
y-m-09-07.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Did you write the reason there are several fixed tables specifically, such as "we don't know which game the 3 students belonged to"?
y-m-09-07.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you look at whether the way to settle on one is going back to the original data to check?
y-m-09-07.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did you say the table you made is a possible table, without stating that it is the right answer?
y-m-09-07.s.s4.model.0: There are several fixed tables because we don't know which games to take the 3 students from. If you recount the slips and check which game counted twice, you can settle on one.
y-m-09-07.s.s4.model.1: The table alone cannot tell which game the 3 students to be reduced belonged to, so several answers come out. You have to make a name list for each game and find the overlapping names.
y-m-09-07.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, point out which number in the previous line the number came from, and whether what the line says is a fact confirmed earlier.
y-m-09-07.s.s2.o.a: Recount the vote slips for each game and match them one by one with the numbers in the table
y-m-09-07.s.s2.r.a: This idea finds where things don't match by checking the table directly against the original data.
y-m-09-07.s.s2.o.b: Change the largest number, 10, to 7 so that the total becomes 28
y-m-09-07.s.s2.r.b: If you only make the total match without checking the reason, you can't tell which game was wrong.
y-m-09-07.s.s2.o.c: Make a list of names for each game and look for students whose names overlap
y-m-09-07.s.s2.r.c: This idea tries to find the overlapping names and confirm the cause.
y-m-09-07.s.s2.o.d: Rewrite the number of students as 31
y-m-09-07.s.s2.r.d: That there are 28 students is a confirmed fact. You are changing a confirmed fact to fit the table.

y-m-09-08.title: What should one picture be worth to make a picture graph easier?
y-m-09-08.topic: Choosing the unit of the pictures in a picture graph
y-m-09-08.goal: Think about the conditions for showing the data values exactly with big and small pictures, confirm that there are several units that fit the conditions, and choose the one that is easier to read, with a reason.
y-m-09-08.material:
You want to show the potato harvests of four fields on a farm in a picture graph. Field 가 is 120 kg, field 나 is 85 kg, field 다 is 45 kg, and field 라 is 30 kg. You use two kinds of pictures: one big picture stands for B kg and one small picture stands for s kg. (kg is read kilogram.) The rules are these.
(1) One big picture must be a bundle of some number of small pictures.
(2) Do not estimate; the harvest must be shown exactly with big and small pictures.
(3) The pictures drawn for one field must not total more than 8.
y-m-09-08.thinking.0: Finding several units that meet the conditions
y-m-09-08.thinking.1: Explaining why a unit does not fit
y-m-09-08.thinking.2: Comparing two designs and giving a reason
y-m-09-08.prereq.0: Reading the numbers that big and small pictures stand for in a picture graph (Grade 3, second semester level)
y-m-09-08.prereq.1: Reading how many small pictures one big picture is a bundle of
y-m-09-08.s.s1.prompt: If one big picture is 100 kg and one small picture is 10 kg, can you show the four harvests following the rules?
y-m-09-08.s.s1.hint.0: Change the four harvests into small pictures (10 kg) only and look for any that cannot be shown exactly.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check which field uses the big picture of 100 kg, and whether the fields that do not use it can be shown with small pictures alone.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.explain: With a 10 kg unit, you cannot show the 5 kg in the ones place of 85 kg and 45 kg. 120 kg and 30 kg are possible, but to show all four harvests exactly, the small picture's unit must divide all four numbers evenly.
y-m-09-08.s.s2.prompt: Make three combinations of a big picture B kg and a small picture s kg, with different big pictures, that follow all of rules (1) to (3).
y-m-09-08.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the number to use for the small picture. Check whether you can show all four harvests as multiples of that number.
y-m-09-08.s.s2.hint.1: Once you have the small picture, pick a big picture and count how many pictures each field from 가 to 라 needs, and check whether it goes over 8.
y-m-09-08.s.s2.ok.c1: B and s are natural numbers and the big picture is bigger.
y-m-09-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make s a natural number that is 1 or more and B a natural number bigger than s.
y-m-09-08.s.s2.ok.c2: One big picture is a bundle of some number of small pictures. (Rule 1)
y-m-09-08.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make B a multiple of s. (Rule 1)
y-m-09-08.s.s2.ok.c3: You can show the four harvests exactly. (Rule 2)
y-m-09-08.s.s2.fail.c3: There is a harvest that cannot be shown exactly with the small picture s. (Rule 2)
y-m-09-08.s.s2.ok.c4: No field has more than 8 pictures. (Rule 3)
y-m-09-08.s.s2.fail.c4: There is a field with more than 8 pictures. (Rule 3) Change the big picture and count again.
y-m-09-08.s.s2.explain: The small picture must show 85, 45, 120, and 30 all exactly, so it must be 5 kg (with 1 kg there would be too many pictures). Big pictures of 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, and 40 kg follow the rules. With 10 kg, field 가 has 12 pictures, and with 50 kg, field 다 has 9 pictures, which goes over 8.
y-m-09-08.s.s3.prompt: Pick two of the units you just made, compare them, and write which is easier for reading the picture graph and why.
y-m-09-08.s.s3.hint.0: For the two units, write the number of pictures needed for field 가 and field 나, put them side by side, and compare.
y-m-09-08.s.s3.hint.1: Also look at the difference between the field with the most pictures and the field with the fewest.
y-m-09-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: ... kg and ... kg are easier. This is because ...
y-m-09-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you actually count the pictures of the four fields with the unit you chose?
y-m-09-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Compared with the other unit, did you say in numbers (the number of pictures) which point is easier?
y-m-09-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about the fact that "easy to read" can differ from person to person?
y-m-09-08.s.s3.model.0: With 40 kg and 5 kg, field 가 is done with 3 big pictures, so there are few pictures and it is easy to count. On the other hand, with 20 kg and 5 kg, field 가 has 6 big pictures, so it is harder to count.
y-m-09-08.s.s3.model.1: 25 kg and 5 kg also work, but field 가 has 4 big pictures and 4 small pictures, 8 in all, which is confusing. With 30 kg and 5 kg, field 가 has only 4 big pictures, so it is easy to read.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.o.a: It can be shown. For 85 kg and 45 kg, cut one 10 kg picture in half and draw a half picture.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.r.a: In the rules, there are only two kinds of pictures, a big picture and a small picture. Making and using a new half picture breaks the rules.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.o.b: It can't be shown. There is a field where the 100 kg big picture is not used, so rule (1) can't be kept.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.r.b: The big picture does not have to be used in every field. A value smaller than the big picture can be shown with only small pictures.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.o.c: It can't be shown. 85 kg and 45 kg don't fit exactly with 10 kg pictures.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.r.c: This idea looked at how the unit of the small picture fits together with the harvest amounts.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.o.d: It can be shown. 30 kg is smaller than the big picture, but it can be shown with 3 small pictures.
y-m-09-08.s.s1.r.d: 30 kg is right, but check whether the harvests of the other fields can all be shown too.

y-m-09-09.title: Can we speak for the whole school from what we asked at the library?
y-m-09-09.topic: The range you can speak about depends on who was surveyed
y-m-09-09.goal: Realize that even if the numbers in the table are right, the range you can speak about depends on who was asked, judge how the survey must change to speak about the whole school, and then rewrite the result to fit the right range.
y-m-09-09.material:
Seou's group wanted to find out "what students at our school most want to do during break time." Seou asked 20 students who were borrowing books at the library during break time and made a table. Our school has about 300 students.
Reading 11 students / Drawing 4 students / Playing on the playground 3 students / Talking with friends 2 students (20 students each chose one.)
Seou said, "So the students at our school most want to read during break time!"
y-m-09-09.thinking.0: Judging the range that the evidence supports
y-m-09-09.thinking.2: Rewriting a conclusion to fit the evidence
y-m-09-09.prereq.0: Reading the number of students for each item from a table and finding the biggest item (Grade 3 level)
y-m-09-09.prereq.1: Knowing the meaning of "the whole school" and "some"
y-m-09-09.s.s1.prompt: What best explains the relationship between Seou's statement and the table?
y-m-09-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write where the 20 students in the table were, and imagine whether the result could differ if you asked the same question to students on the playground.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether "the students at our school" in Seou's sentence and the "20 students" in the table are the same group.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.explain: The numbers in the table are the story of the 20 students we met at the library. Students who come to the library are likely to like reading, so you cannot say it shows the thinking of the whole school as it is. Even if you add more people, asking in the same place leaves the same problem.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.prompt: To get a result you can speak about for the whole school, how would it be good to change the survey? Choose all the fitting methods.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.hint.0: For each method, write which students at the school would be left out if you asked that way.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.hint.1: Mark the methods where no students are left out or where many different students are included evenly.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.r.a: This thinking makes sure many different students in the school are included evenly.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.o.b: Ask only the students playing on the playground during break time.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.r.b: Only the place changed, from the library to the playground, and it is the same in that you ask only one side's students.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.o.c: Have all the students in the school write their answer to the same question on a slip and hand it in.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.r.c: This thinking puts every student in the school into the survey group.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.o.d: Ask the 20 closest friends the same question.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.r.d: Close friends often have similar thoughts, so it is hard for them to represent the whole school.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.o.e: Pick 20 students who seem likely to answer well and ask them.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.r.e: If the person doing the survey picks, the thinking can lean to one side.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.explain: Picking evenly from each class and asking, or asking all students in the school, includes the school's many students with none left out. Asking only students in one place, close friends, or students picked by the person doing the survey can lean to one side.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.acc.0: Picking evenly and asking is also good. But you must decide how many to pick from each class and how. It would be even better to also choose the method of asking all students in the school.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.acc.1: Asking all students in the school is also good. It takes a long time and some students may not hand in a slip. It would be even better to also choose the method of picking evenly and asking.
y-m-09-09.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Seou's last statement to fit the range the table shows. Write it so that who was asked and the numbers in the table are visible.
y-m-09-09.s.s3.hint.0: In Seou's sentence, change the words "the students at our school" to the group that appears in the table.
y-m-09-09.s.s3.hint.1: Put the numbers you can say from the table (the biggest item and its number of students) into the sentence.
y-m-09-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Can you find "who was asked" in your sentence and underline it?
y-m-09-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you put the numbers from the table in the sentence?
y-m-09-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If there is a part that speaks about the whole school, is there evidence to say so?
y-m-09-09.s.s3.model.0: Among the 20 students we met at the library, 11 said they most want to read during break time. We did not ask the whole school, so we cannot say that the whole school feels the same.
y-m-09-09.s.s3.model.1: When we asked 20 students who came to borrow books, reading was the most with 11. If we also ask students on the playground, a different result may come out.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.o.a: Reading books is the most with 11 students, so it is also the most among all students in the school.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.r.a: This idea takes the largest number in the table as the largest number for the whole school. Read again whose results the table shows.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.o.b: These are the results of 20 students who came to the library, so they can't be carried over as they are to all students in the school.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.r.b: This idea checks whose results the table shows and sets the range of what can be said.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.o.c: We asked all 20 students, so it is also true for all students in the school.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.r.c: You need to look at who was asked, not at how many students were asked.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.o.d: 20 is too few, so if we ask 100 students we can say something about all students in the school.
y-m-09-09.s.s1.r.d: Just increasing the number of people does not solve it. What kind of students the 100 are may matter more.
y-m-09-09.s.s2.o.a: Pick a few students from each class by drawing lots and ask them the same question

y-m-09-10.title: When we know only the totals, can we decide how many stickers are in each cell?
y-m-09-10.topic: Finding the blank cells in a table sorted by two rules
y-m-09-10.goal: Think about whether the numbers in the cells are settled to one when only the totals are given, make several tables that fit the conditions, and sort out which new clue settles it to one.
y-m-09-10.material: 12 stickers were sorted by color (red, blue) and shape (circle, star). All we know are the totals. There are 7 red stickers and 5 blue stickers, and 8 circles and 4 stars. We do not yet know how many stickers are in each of the table's four cells (red circle, red star, blue circle, blue star). Every sticker has one color and one shape.
y-m-09-10.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-09-10.thinking.1: Making several cases that fit the conditions
y-m-09-10.prereq.0: Showing sorted counts in a table and finding the totals (Grade 3 level)
y-m-09-10.prereq.1: Sorting things by two rules, such as color and shape
y-m-09-10.s.s1.prompt: From the totals alone, can you know exactly how many stickers are in each of the four cells?
y-m-09-10.s.s1.hint.0: Suppose red circle is 3 stickers, write how many the other cells would be, and check that all four totals fit.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.hint.1: Change red circle to other numbers, do the same, and look for other cases where all the totals fit.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.o.a: You can. There are 7 red, so red circle is 7, and the rest are settled in order.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.r.a: This decided that all 7 red are circles. Check whether some of the red could be stars.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.o.b: You can. Splitting 12 equally among four cells gives 3 in each cell.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.r.b: There is no condition anywhere that the cells are equal. Also check whether the totals fit.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.o.c: You cannot. Even with the same totals, there can be several ways to split among the cells.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.r.c: This thinking looked for other splits that fit the totals.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.o.d: You cannot. There is nothing you can say about any cell.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.r.d: Even if you do not know the exact value, you can state the range of possible numbers for each cell.
y-m-09-10.s.s1.explain: It is not settled how many of the 7 red are circles, so even with the same totals, different splits among the cells are possible. Still, you can state the range of possible numbers for each cell.
y-m-09-10.s.s2.prompt: Make three tables, with different numbers of red circles, that keep all four totals (red 7, blue 5, circle 8, star 4).
y-m-09-10.s.s2.hint.0: Put a number in the red circle cell, then fill in red star, blue circle, and blue star in that order, matching the totals.
y-m-09-10.s.s2.hint.1: When you change red circle, check that no cell becomes negative and no total is off.
y-m-09-10.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers in the cells are natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-09-10.s.s2.fail.c1: Please write the number of stickers as a natural number that is 0 or more.
y-m-09-10.s.s2.fail.c2: Red circle and red star together must be 7.
y-m-09-10.s.s2.fail.c3: Blue circle and blue star together must be 5.
y-m-09-10.s.s2.fail.c4: Red circle and blue circle together must be 8.
y-m-09-10.s.s2.fail.c5: Red star and blue star together must be 4.
y-m-09-10.s.s2.explain: If red circle is 3, then (3, 4, 5, 0), if 4 then (4, 3, 4, 1), if 5 then (5, 2, 3, 2), if 6 then (6, 1, 2, 3), and if 7 then (7, 0, 1, 4) keep all the totals. Once red circle is settled, the other three cells follow, and red circle can be from 3 to 7, so there are 5 ways in all.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.prompt: Choose all the cases where, if you learned one more new fact, all four cells would be settled to one.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.hint.0: Apply the fact in each choice to the five tables above one at a time and count how many tables that fit the fact remain.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.hint.1: Find and mark the choices where exactly one table remains.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.o.a: There is not a single blue star sticker.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.r.a: This thinking checked how many of the five tables remain with blue star at 0.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.o.b: Red circle is more than blue circle.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.r.b: The tables with red circle at 5, 6, or 7 all fit. It is still not settled to one.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.o.c: Red star is more than blue star.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.r.c: The tables with red circle at 3 and at 4 both fit. It is still not settled to one.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.o.d: Red circle and blue circle have the same number.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.r.d: This thinking checked whether, if the 8 circles are split equally between the two colors, the other cells follow.
y-m-09-10.s.s3.explain: If blue star is 0, red star is 4 and red circle is 3, so it is settled as (3, 4, 5, 0). If red circle and blue circle are the same, each is 4, so it is settled as (4, 3, 4, 1). For b and c, several fitting tables remain.

y-m-09-11.title: Can we tell who won while the votes are still being counted?
y-m-09-11.topic: When to judge a result while data keeps building up
y-m-09-11.goal: Learn that with only part of the data counted you cannot yet settle the result, and that thinking about whether the ranking could flip with the remaining data lets you find a point where it can be settled.
y-m-09-11.material: In a class meeting, we voted to choose our class's representative animal. The candidates are three: rabbit, turtle, and sparrow, and 30 students voted in all. Everyone cast one vote and there are no invalid votes. The teacher opens the votes one at a time to count them and tells us the results from time to time. The candidate with the most votes becomes the representative animal.
y-m-09-11.thinking.0: Judging the range you can speak about with the data so far
y-m-09-11.thinking.1: Fixing your judgment when new data comes in
y-m-09-11.thinking.2: Explaining the conditions needed to settle a result
y-m-09-11.prereq.0: Reading and comparing the number for each item from a table (Grade 3 level)
y-m-09-11.prereq.1: Thinking about how many votes are not yet counted from the total number of votes and the number already counted
y-m-09-11.s.s1.prompt: The counting results are announced at each stage. Each time, choose your thinking.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.hint.0: At each stage, write side by side the vote difference between the first-place and second-place candidates and the number of votes not yet opened.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.hint.1: Suppose all the remaining votes go to the second-place candidate and check with numbers whether it passes first place.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.info: 10 votes have been opened. Rabbit has 5 votes, turtle 3 votes, and sparrow 2 votes. There are 20 votes not yet opened.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can we say at this point that rabbit has been decided as the representative animal?
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.after: Rabbit is ahead, but there are still 20 votes not yet opened, so the result could flip.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It's decided, because rabbit has the most right now.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Being ahead now and being ahead to the end are different. Think about how many votes are not yet opened.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It's decided, because half of the 10 opened votes are for rabbit.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Half of the opened votes does not mean half of all 30 votes.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Turtle will win. It will catch up soon.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This guesses the votes we don't know yet in favor of one side.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is not decided yet. 20 votes are still left unopened.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This thinking considered whether the remaining votes could change the result.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.info: 20 votes have been opened. Rabbit has 9 votes, turtle 7 votes, and sparrow 4 votes. There are 10 votes not yet opened.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.ask: Choose all the statements that describe the situation now correctly.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.after: If turtle or sparrow gets many of the remaining 10 votes, it could flip. We cannot settle it yet, but it is fine to say that rabbit has the advantage.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Rabbit has been decided as the representative animal, because it is ahead by 2 votes.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Check whether the remaining 10 votes could flip the 2-vote difference.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Turtle can't win anymore. It has fewer than rabbit.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Calculate what happens if turtle gets many of the remaining 10 votes.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Rabbit is ahead, but another candidate could win with the remaining 10 votes.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This thinking looks together at being ahead now and whether the remaining votes could flip it.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Sparrow can't win. It has the fewest.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.r.d: If sparrow gets all the remaining 10 votes, it has 14 votes. The fact that it has few now cannot rule out the possibility.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.o.e: Rabbit looks likely to win, but it is not settled yet.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.1.r.e: This thinking keeps that it is not settled while still stating how likely it is.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.info: 27 votes have been opened. Rabbit has 14 votes, turtle 9 votes, and sparrow 4 votes. There are 3 votes not yet opened.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.ask: Can we now say that rabbit has been decided as the representative animal?
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.after: The remaining 3 votes are fewer than the vote difference between rabbit and turtle (5 votes), so the result cannot flip. Even with unopened votes remaining, you can settle it.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It's decided. Even if turtle gets all the remaining 3 votes, it has 12, which does not pass 14.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This thinking checks whether the ranking changes even when you assume the remaining votes go in the worst way.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It's decided, because rabbit has the most votes now.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The conclusion is right, but you could have said the same thing at the start when it was ahead. You need a reason that takes the remaining votes into account.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is not decided yet, because there are still unopened votes.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Just that there are remaining votes does not tell you whether the result could change. Compare the number of remaining votes with the vote difference.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It is not decided yet. Sparrow could get all the remaining 3 votes.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Even if sparrow gets all 3 votes, it has 7, which does not pass rabbit. Calculate the possible cases yourself.
y-m-09-11.s.s1.reflect: At 10 votes and 20 votes, many votes remained and the result could flip, so "we don't know yet" was fitting. At 27 votes, the number of remaining votes was smaller than the vote difference between first and second place, so it could be settled. To settle it, you must look together at how far ahead it is now and how many votes remain. Say at which step and how your thinking changed.
y-m-09-11.s.s2.prompt: While counting votes, to say "the representative has been decided now," which numbers should you look at? Write using the 27-vote moment above as an example.
y-m-09-11.s.s2.hint.0: Write the vote difference between first and second place and put it side by side with the number of remaining votes.
y-m-09-11.s.s2.hint.1: Write with numbers the case where the second place takes all the remaining votes.
y-m-09-11.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include both the number of remaining votes and the vote difference between first and second place?
y-m-09-11.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check by using the numbers at the 27-vote moment (14, 9, 3)?
y-m-09-11.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you think about what would happen when the remaining votes equal the difference?
y-m-09-11.s.s2.model.0: Compare the votes the first place has with the votes the second place would have if it took all the remaining votes. If the second place still cannot pass the first place even after taking all the remaining votes, the first place is settled. At 27 votes, turtle would have 9+3=12 votes, which does not pass rabbit's 14 votes.
y-m-09-11.s.s2.model.1: If the number of remaining votes is smaller than the vote difference between first and second place, it can't be flipped, so it has won. At 27 votes the difference is 5 votes and the remaining votes are 3, so it can't catch up.

y-m-09-12.title: Shall we make a question that the table alone cannot answer?
y-m-09-12.topic: What you can learn from the table alone and what you need to know more
y-m-09-12.goal: Separate statements you can answer with the numbers in the table from those that need more knowledge, then make a question yourself that the table alone cannot answer and say what more is needed.
y-m-09-12.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-09-12.prereq.0: Reading and comparing the number for each item from a table (Grade 3 level)
y-m-09-12.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the statements (or questions) you can answer from the table alone.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.hint.0: For each statement, write which numbers in the table are used to check it.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.hint.1: Mark the statements that need numbers that are not in the table.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.o.a: How many students in Class 2 do not wear glasses?
y-m-09-12.s.s1.r.a: To know the number of students not wearing glasses, you need the total number of students in Class 2, but it is not in the table.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.o.b: The class with the most students wearing glasses is Class 2.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.r.b: This thinking compared the three numbers in the table directly.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.o.c: In Class 2, the share of students wearing glasses is bigger than in Class 1.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.r.c: To compare shares, you need the total number of students in both classes. They are not in the table.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.o.d: If you put all three classes together, 20 students wear glasses.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.r.d: This thinking gathered all three numbers.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.o.e: The numbers of students wearing glasses in Class 1 and Class 3 differ by 1.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.r.e: This thinking compared two numbers and looked at the difference.
y-m-09-12.s.s1.explain: b, d, and e can be checked with the numbers in the table alone. a and c need the total number of students in each class, so the table alone cannot answer them.
y-m-09-12.s.s2.prompt: Make one question that this table alone cannot answer, and write what more you need to know to answer it.
y-m-09-12.s.s2.hint.0: Compare with questions that can be answered directly with the numbers in the table, and think of a question where you need to know one more thing.
y-m-09-12.s.s2.hint.1: Write what number you would need to answer that question.
y-m-09-12.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Is it ...? I need to know ...
y-m-09-12.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the answer to your question really cannot be settled by the numbers in the table alone?
y-m-09-12.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write specifically what more you need to know (like "the total number of students")?
y-m-09-12.s.s2.selfAssess.2: If that information were available, could you answer the question?
y-m-09-12.s.s2.model.0: How many students in Class 2 do not wear glasses? I need to know how many students there are in Class 2 in all.
y-m-09-12.s.s2.model.1: Which class has the biggest share of students wearing glasses? I need the total number of students in each class.
y-m-09-12.s.s2.model.2: How many students will wear glasses tomorrow? I need data surveyed tomorrow.
y-m-09-12.material: We surveyed the number of students wearing glasses in three third-grade classes and organized it in a table. Class 1 has 6, Class 2 has 9, and Class 3 has 5.
y-m-09-12.s.s2.model.3: How many students in Class 2 do not wear glasses? We need to be told the total number of students in Class 2.

y-m-09-13.title: Can I write "most students like pizza"?
y-m-09-13.topic: Checking whether a sentence interpreting a table matches the table, and rewriting it
y-m-09-13.goal: Separate sentences that the numbers in the table support from sentences that exaggerate, and rewrite the exaggerated sentence to fit the facts so that readers are not misled.
y-m-09-13.material: 30 Grade 3 students each chose one favorite lunch menu. The results are pizza 9 students, chicken 8 students, bibimbap 7 students, and noodles 6 students. One student wrote a draft of an article for the school newspaper. This newspaper is read by first-grade younger students too.
y-m-09-13.thinking.0: Evaluating whether a sentence has gone further than the evidence
y-m-09-13.thinking.1: Deciding the meaning of words like "most"
y-m-09-13.prereq.0: Reading the number of students for each item from a table and finding the biggest item (Grade 3 level)
y-m-09-13.prereq.1: Knowing how much half of the total is
y-m-09-13.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in the draft that the table alone does not support.
y-m-09-13.s.s1.hint.0: Find the numbers in each line in the table and check whether they are right.
y-m-09-13.s.s1.hint.1: Put the number of students who chose pizza and the number who did not side by side and compare.
y-m-09-13.s.s1.line.0: 30 Grade 3 students each chose one favorite lunch menu.
y-m-09-13.s.s1.line.2: Most of the students like pizza.
y-m-09-13.s.s1.explain: Line 3 goes further than the table. 9 of the 30 students chose pizza, so the other 21 chose other menus. Being the most and being most of them are different. Lines 1, 2, and 4 match the table.
y-m-09-13.s.s2.prompt: To write "most students chose pizza," about how many students at least would have to choose pizza?
y-m-09-13.s.s2.hint.0: Find how many students are half of 30 and compare that number with the number who chose pizza.
y-m-09-13.s.s2.o.a: 9 is enough, because it is the most.
y-m-09-13.s.s2.r.a: This thinking treats the most and most of them as the same meaning.
y-m-09-13.s.s2.o.b: 15 is enough, because it is half of 30.
